I used **the full argument and main content of the poem**, but I did **not** use every original line word-for-word.

## What I did

I adapted the poem into a **song lyric version** by:

- keeping the central refrain idea: **“plain-dealing man”**
- preserving the main moral targets:
  - swaggerers
  - flatterers / dissemblers
  - gossipers / meddling tongues
  - malicious neighbours
  - false swearers
  - bribe-takers
  - cheats and thieves
  - wasteful young people
  - bad company
  - keeping conscience and trust
- compressing and reshaping the poem into a **Gilbert-style theatrical song**
- adding new phrasing, patter lines, ensemble responses, and stage-friendly sections

## What I did not do

I did **not** make a line-by-line complete lyrical setting of every stanza in the original.

Some original lines were:

- paraphrased
- condensed
- modernised
- rearranged
- replaced with more singable lines
- expanded into new comic/patter material

## Exact answer

The version I gave is a **free adaptation**, not a complete preservation of the original lyrics.

For your project, there are two possible routes:

| Version type | Best for | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Full-faithful version** | preserving the whole historical poem | longer, more archaic, less commercial |
| **Adapted Gilbert version** | making it work as a theatrical song | stronger musically, but not every line is preserved |

For the **Gilbert project**, the adapted version is better musically.  
For archival or legal-style completeness, a **full-faithful song version** would be better.

Yes. It is a **good idea**.

It helps because Suno is less likely to get confused when:

- the **vocal/production directions are listed once**
- the **song order is clear**
- the lyrics do not repeat long instructions in every heading
- repeated chorus sections are marked simply as **same chorus**
- the final section is not split into three separate “final verse” labels

## Best format for your case

Use **two blocks**:

### 1. Production/vocal map

This tells Suno what each delivery style means.

```text
baritone operetta vocal, used for intro, moral pre-choruses, final moral resolution, outro
hip-hop spoken operetta mix, used for verse 1, bribery verse, practical advice lines
gilbertian patter rap, used for flatterer verse, busy tongues verse, oath-made knave verse
ensemble chorus, used for main chorus and repeat chorus
ensemble response, used for short crowd replies and chants
spoken baritone, used for comic warning transitions
rap-cabaret bridge, used for fastest slippery men catalogue
grand ensemble operetta rap, used for final chant and finale
```

### 2. Lyrics with short section labels

Then in the lyrics use only compact labels:

```text
intro, baritone operetta vocal
verse 1, hip-hop spoken operetta mix
pre-chorus, baritone operetta vocal
chorus, ensemble chorus
verse 2, gilbertian patter rap
ensemble response
verse 3, gilbertian patter rap
repeat chorus, same chorus
```

## My judgement

This is better than long headings like:

```text
[VERSE 2 — GILBERTIAN PATTER RAP: fast, articulate, comic rhythmic delivery; halfway between operetta patter song and rap flow]
```

That kind of long heading wastes characters and can confuse the model.

Your idea gives Suno a cleaner command structure:

> **First: define the vocal tools.  
> Second: tell it where to use them.  
> Third: give the lyrics.**

That is the strongest layout for a long song with multiple vocal styles.

THE PLAIN-DEALING MAN.

[The oldest copy of the Plain Dealing Man with which we have been able to meet is in black letter, printed by T. Vere at the sign ‘Of the Angel without Newgate.’  Vere was living in 1609.]
A crotchet comes into my mind
Concerning a proverb of old,
Plain dealing’s a jewel most rare,
And more precious than silver or gold:
And therefore with patience give ear,
And listen to what here is penned,
These verses were written on purpose
The honest man’s cause to defend.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
Yet some are so impudent grown,
They’ll domineer, vapour, and swagger,
And say that the plain-dealing man
Was born to die a beggar:
p. 12But men that are honestly given
Do such evil actions detest,
And every one that is well-minded

## Modern-English paraphrase  
### **The Plain-Dealing Man**

A thought has come into my mind about an old proverb:

**“Plain dealing is a rare jewel, more valuable than silver or gold.”**

So please listen patiently to what I have written. These verses were made to defend the cause of the honest man.

I will show clearly, and prove from experience, that the best thing in the world is to be a straightforward and honest man.

---

Some people have become so shameless that they boast, bully, show off, and swagger. They say that an honest, plain-dealing man is destined to become poor.

But people who are truly honest hate such bad behaviour. Any decent-minded person will agree that honesty is best.

So I will show again, from experience, that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

As for me, I am a poor man. Sometimes I barely have a shilling to my name.

Even so, God knows I truly want to live honestly in the world.

My clothes may be worn out, and my job may be humble and lowly, but I will still do my best to keep hunger and poverty away from my door.

That is why I say: the best thing in the world is to be an honest, straightforward man.

---

Now I will speak plainly and briefly. I will tell you exactly what I think, what kind of person I am, and what I am inclined toward.

I hate deceitful, low-minded rogues. I hate flatterers and people who try to win favour dishonestly.

As for painted-faced prostitutes and similar people, they will never get a penny from me.

For I maintain that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

I also cannot stand people who talk too much and gossip without reason about things that do not concern them.

Such behaviour is dangerous and almost treasonous.

So I advise everyone listening: do not meddle in matters of government or state affairs, or you may be questioned about it and regret it when it is too late.

Again, I say: the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

Shame on spiteful neighbours whose malicious nature drives them to harm innocent poor people every day.

Because of people like them, many good men have been ruined, and their wives and children have suffered as well.

This is another reason why honest dealing is best.

---

Shame on false, perjured men who have no conscience.

They swear and break their oaths constantly, almost every third word they speak.

As long as they can gain profit, they do not care what lies they tell.

Such cursed deceivers are worse than devils.

This proves again that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

Shame on greedy people who take bribes.

It is a pity they were ever born, because they are like caterpillars destroying the fruits of the earth.

They take money with both hands, from one side and from the other.

They do not care whom they ruin — even if it is their own father or brother.

That is why I say again: the best thing in the world is to be an honest man.

---

Shame on cheats and thieves who live by fraud and deceit.

The gallows waits for people like them, and the hangman waits for their clothes.

Although poverty is shameful and hardship is painful, it is better to live like a beggar than to be carried in a cart as a condemned thief.

So I repeat: the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

Now let all honest people judge whether the kinds of people I have named deserve blame for their wicked and shameless behaviour.

Before I finish, I will give the world one piece of advice, which may guide some people onto the right path and teach them to live better.

I have now shown clearly, and many people can witness it, that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

First, beware of the company you keep.

Wicked people can quickly tempt others into sin.

---

Second, if young people inherit or receive wealth, with plenty of silver and gold, they should save some of it for later life, so they will have comfort when they grow old.

---

Third, I have known many young wasteful people who spent their money so quickly that they later fell into poverty and were forced to beg.

---

Fourth, I advise all people to keep a clear conscience and act justly in everything they do.

A person is truly a false villain if he cannot be trusted with what has been given into his care.

---

And now I will end my song and bring it to a proper conclusion.

I have told you what is in my mind and what my firm resolution is.

I have shown, and I can prove from experience, that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

## Best version to make it a song

The **best version is not the full original poem unchanged**. It is too long and too sermon-like for a modern song.

The strongest musical version would be a **compressed adaptation** built around the refrain:

> **’Tis the excellent thing in the world  
> To be a plain-dealing man**

That refrain is the hook. The song should keep the old moral-ballad flavour but reduce the verses into selected “character attacks”:

1. **boasters / swaggerers**
2. **false swearers / liars**
3. **bribe takers**
4. **cheaters / thieves**
5. **final moral advice**

That gives the song shape instead of becoming a long list.

---

## Best genre

### Best fit: **Victorian music-hall / comic moral ballad**

This fits the **Gilbert project** best if you mean a Gilbert & Sullivan / W. S. Gilbert-style piece.

Why it works:

- The poem already has a **comic moral lecturer** voice.
- It attacks social types: hypocrites, gossips, bribe-takers, cheats.
- The repeated refrain can become a **catchy chorus**.
- The speaker sounds self-righteous but slightly ridiculous, which is very Gilbertian.
- It can be staged as a character song: one man presenting himself as “the honest man” while judging everyone else.

### Secondary fit: **patter-song / satirical catalogue song**

This would be more comic and faster.

The repeated “O fie upon…” sections could become a patter catalogue:

> O fie upon the bribe-taker,  
> oath-breaker, coin-shaker,  
> back-door favour-maker,  
> truth-bending man...

This would sync strongly with Gilbert-style social satire.

---

## Suggested song concept for the Gilbert project

### Title

**“The Plain-Dealing Man”**

### Character

A pompous but sincere lower-middle-class moralist.  
He believes he is the last honest man in a corrupt world.

### Tone

Comic, moral, theatrical, slightly self-important.

### Musical style

- **Light operetta / Victorian music hall**
- 6/8 or jaunty 2/4
- March-like chorus
- Increasingly fast verse sections
- Ensemble can echo the refrain mock-seriously

---

## Best structure

```text
[INTRO]
Short spoken or sung setup:
“A crotchet comes into my mind...”

[VERSE 1]
He introduces the proverb:
Plain dealing is rarer than gold.

[CHORUS]
For this I make it clear as I can,
The finest thing in life is a plain-dealing man.

[VERSE 2]
Attack on swaggerers, flatterers, liars.

[CHORUS]

[VERSE 3]
Attack on bribe-takers, cheats, thieves.

[CHORUS]

[BRIDGE / PATTER SECTION]
Fast comic list of every dishonest type.

[FINAL VERSE]
Advice to young men:
avoid bad company, save your money, keep conscience clean.

[FINAL CHORUS]
Bigger, ensemble, comic-moral finish.
```

---

## What I would avoid

Do **not** make it:

- a solemn folk ballad only
- a modern pop song
- a dark dramatic aria
- a fully literal setting of every stanza

The material is moral and repetitive, so if treated too seriously it may become dull. It needs **comic theatrical energy**.

---

## Best adapted chorus

A stronger singable chorus could be:

```text
For I’ll make it appear,
As plainly as I can,
There’s nothing half so rare
As a plain-dealing man.
Let silver go to rust,
Let gold slip through the hand,
The jewel of the world
Is a plain-dealing man.
```

This keeps the old idea but makes it more musical.

---

## My recommendation

For the Gilbert project, make it a **comic operetta character song**:

> **Genre:** Victorian music-hall operetta / Gilbertian patter ballad  
> **Mood:** witty, moral, theatrical, satirical  
> **Voice:** pompous honest man condemning a corrupt society  
> **Best use:** Act I character introduction or comic moral set-piece

## **THE PLAIN-DEALING MAN**

```text
[TITLE]
THE PLAIN-DEALING MAN

[SOURCE NOTE]
From Ancient Poems, Ballads and Songs of the Peasantry of England,
edited by Robert Bell.
The note to the poem states that the oldest copy known to the editor was
a black-letter copy printed by T. Vere at the sign “Of the Angel without Newgate.”

[ORIGINAL TEXT]

A crotchet comes into my mind
Concerning a proverb of old,
Plain dealing’s a jewel most rare,
And more precious than silver or gold:
And therefore with patience give ear,
And listen to what here is penned,
These verses were written on purpose
The honest man’s cause to defend.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

Yet some are so impudent grown,
They’ll domineer, vapour, and swagger,
And say that the plain-dealing man
Was born to die a beggar:
But men that are honestly given
Do such evil actions detest,
And every one that is well-minded
Will say that plain dealing is best.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

For my part I am a poor man,
And sometimes scarce muster a shilling,
Yet to live upright in the world,
Heaven knows I am wondrous willing.
Although that my clothes be threadbare,
And my calling be simple and poor,
Yet will I endeavour myself
To keep off the wolf from the door.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

And now, to be brief in discourse,
In plain terms I’ll tell you my mind;
My qualities you shall all know,
And to what my humour’s inclined:
I hate all dissembling base knaves
And pickthanks whoever they be,
And for painted-faced drabs, and such like,
They shall never get penny of me.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

Nor can I abide any tongues
That will prattle and prate against reason,
About that which doth not concern them;
Which thing is no better than treason.
Wherefore I’d wish all that do hear me
Not to meddle with matters of state,
Lest they be in question called for it,
And repent them when it is too late.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon spiteful neighbours,
Whose malicious humours are bent,
And do practise and strive every day
To wrong the poor innocent.
By means of such persons as they,
There hath many a good mother’s son
Been utterly brought to decay,
Their wives and their children undone.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon forsworn knaves,
That do no conscience make
To swear and forswear themselves
At every third word they do speak:
So they may get profit and gain,
They care not what lies they do tell;
Such cursed dissemblers as they
Are worse than the devils of hell.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon greedy bribe takers,
’Tis pity they ever drew breath,
For they, like to base caterpillars,
Devour up the fruits of the earth.
They’re apt to take money with both hands,
On one side and also the other,
And care not what men they undo,
Though it be their own father or brother.

Therefore I will make it appear,
And show very good reasons I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon cheaters and thieves,
That liveth by fraud and deceit;
The gallows do for such blades groan,
And the hangmen do for their clothes wait.
Though poverty be a disgrace,
And want is a pitiful grief,
’Tis better to go like a beggar
Than to ride in a cart like a thief.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

And now let all honest men judge,
If such men as I have here named
For their wicked and impudent dealings,
Deserveth not much to be blamed.
And now here, before I conclude,
One item to the world I will give,
Which may direct some the right way,
And teach them the better to live.

For now I have made it appear,
And many men witness it can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

1. I’ th’ first place I’d wish you beware
What company you come in,
For those that are wicked themselves
May quickly tempt others to sin.

2. If youths be inducèd with wealth,
And have plenty of silver and gold,
I’d wish them keep something in store,
To comfort them when they are old.

3. I have known many young prodigals,
Which have wasted their money so fast,
That they have been driven in want,
And were forcèd to beg at the last.

4. I’d wish all men bear a good conscience,
And in all their actions be just;
For he’s a false varlet indeed
That will not be true to his trust.

And now to conclude my new song,
And draw to a perfect conclusion,
I have told you what is in my mind,
And what is my firm resolution.

For this I have made it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
```

Poems.

THE PLAIN-DEALING MAN.

[The oldest copy of the Plain Dealing Man with which we have been able to meet is in black letter, printed by T. Vere at the sign ‘Of the Angel without Newgate.’  Vere was living in 1609.]
A crotchet comes into my mind
Concerning a proverb of old,
Plain dealing’s a jewel most rare,
And more precious than silver or gold:
And therefore with patience give ear,
And listen to what here is penned,
These verses were written on purpose
The honest man’s cause to defend.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
Yet some are so impudent grown,
They’ll domineer, vapour, and swagger,
And say that the plain-dealing man
Was born to die a beggar:
p. 12But men that are honestly given
Do such evil actions detest,
And every one that is well-minded
Will say that plain dealing is best.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
For my part I am a poor man,
And sometimes scarce muster a shilling,
Yet to live upright in the world,
Heaven knows I am wondrous willing.
Although that my clothes be threadbare,
And my calling be simple and poor,
Yet will I endeavour myself
To keep off the wolf from the door.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
And now, to be brief in discourse,
In plain terms I’ll tell you my mind;
My qualities you shall all know,
And to what my humour’s inclined:
I hate all dissembling base knaves
And pickthanks whoever they be,
And for painted-faced drabs, and such like,
They shall never get penny of me.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
Nor can I abide any tongues
That will prattle and prate against reason,
About that which doth not concern them;
Which thing is no better than treason.
p. 13Wherefore I’d wish all that do hear me
Not to meddle with matters of state,
Lest they be in question called for it,
And repent them when it is too late.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
O fie upon spiteful neighbours,
Whose malicious humours are bent,
And do practise and strive every day
To wrong the poor innocent.
By means of such persons as they,
There hath many a good mother’s son
Been utterly brought to decay,
Their wives and their children undone.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
O fie upon forsworn knaves,
That do no conscience make
To swear and forswear themselves
At every third word they do speak:
So they may get profit and gain,
They care not what lies they do tell;
Such cursed dissemblers as they
Are worse than the devils of hell.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
O fie upon greedy bribe takers,
’Tis pity they ever drew breath,
For they, like to base caterpillars,
Devour up the fruits of the earth.
p. 14They’re apt to take money with both hands,
On one side and also the other,
And care not what men they undo,
Though it be their own father or brother.
Therefore I will make it appear,
And show very good reasons I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
O fie upon cheaters and thieves,
That liveth by fraud and deceit;
The gallows do for such blades groan,
And the hangmen do for their clothes wait.
Though poverty be a disgrace,
And want is a pitiful grief,
’Tis better to go like a beggar
Than to ride in a cart like a thief.
For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
And now let all honest men judge,
If such men as I have here named
For their wicked and impudent dealings,
Deserveth not much to be blamed.
And now here, before I conclude,
One item to the world I will give,
Which may direct some the right way,
And teach them the better to live.
For now I have made it appear,
And many men witness it can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.
1.  I’ th’ first place I’d wish you beware
What company you come in,
For those that are wicked themselves
May quickly tempt others to sin.
p. 152.  If youths be inducèd with wealth,
And have plenty of silver and gold,
I’d wish them keep something in store,
To comfort them when they are old.
3.  I have known many young prodigals,
Which have wasted their money so fast,
That they have been driven in want,
And were forcèd to beg at the last.
4.  I’d wish all men bear a good conscience,
And in all their actions be just;
For he’s a false varlet indeed
That will not be true to his trust.
And now to conclude my new song,
And draw to a perfect conclusion,
I have told you what is in my mind,
And what is my [firm] resolution.
For this I have made it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

## Modern-English paraphrase  
### **The Plain-Dealing Man**

A thought has come into my mind about an old proverb:

**“Plain dealing is a rare jewel, more valuable than silver or gold.”**

So please listen patiently to what I have written. These verses were made to defend the cause of the honest man.

I will show clearly, and prove from experience, that the best thing in the world is to be a straightforward and honest man.

---

Some people have become so shameless that they boast, bully, show off, and swagger. They say that an honest, plain-dealing man is destined to become poor.

But people who are truly honest hate such bad behaviour. Any decent-minded person will agree that honesty is best.

So I will show again, from experience, that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

As for me, I am a poor man. Sometimes I barely have a shilling to my name.

Even so, God knows I truly want to live honestly in the world.

My clothes may be worn out, and my job may be humble and lowly, but I will still do my best to keep hunger and poverty away from my door.

That is why I say: the best thing in the world is to be an honest, straightforward man.

---

Now I will speak plainly and briefly. I will tell you exactly what I think, what kind of person I am, and what I am inclined toward.

I hate deceitful, low-minded rogues. I hate flatterers and people who try to win favour dishonestly.

As for painted-faced prostitutes and similar people, they will never get a penny from me.

For I maintain that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

I also cannot stand people who talk too much and gossip without reason about things that do not concern them.

Such behaviour is dangerous and almost treasonous.

So I advise everyone listening: do not meddle in matters of government or state affairs, or you may be questioned about it and regret it when it is too late.

Again, I say: the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

Shame on spiteful neighbours whose malicious nature drives them to harm innocent poor people every day.

Because of people like them, many good men have been ruined, and their wives and children have suffered as well.

This is another reason why honest dealing is best.

---

Shame on false, perjured men who have no conscience.

They swear and break their oaths constantly, almost every third word they speak.

As long as they can gain profit, they do not care what lies they tell.

Such cursed deceivers are worse than devils.

This proves again that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

Shame on greedy people who take bribes.

It is a pity they were ever born, because they are like caterpillars destroying the fruits of the earth.

They take money with both hands, from one side and from the other.

They do not care whom they ruin — even if it is their own father or brother.

That is why I say again: the best thing in the world is to be an honest man.

---

Shame on cheats and thieves who live by fraud and deceit.

The gallows waits for people like them, and the hangman waits for their clothes.

Although poverty is shameful and hardship is painful, it is better to live like a beggar than to be carried in a cart as a condemned thief.

So I repeat: the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

Now let all honest people judge whether the kinds of people I have named deserve blame for their wicked and shameless behaviour.

Before I finish, I will give the world one piece of advice, which may guide some people onto the right path and teach them to live better.

I have now shown clearly, and many people can witness it, that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

---

First, beware of the company you keep.

Wicked people can quickly tempt others into sin.

---

Second, if young people inherit or receive wealth, with plenty of silver and gold, they should save some of it for later life, so they will have comfort when they grow old.

---

Third, I have known many young wasteful people who spent their money so quickly that they later fell into poverty and were forced to beg.

---

Fourth, I advise all people to keep a clear conscience and act justly in everything they do.

A person is truly a false villain if he cannot be trusted with what has been given into his care.

---

And now I will end my song and bring it to a proper conclusion.

I have told you what is in my mind and what my firm resolution is.

I have shown, and I can prove from experience, that the best thing in the world is to be a plain-dealing man.

## Source confirmed

The link is to Project Gutenberg eBook **#649**, titled:

**_Ancient Poems, Ballads and Songs of the Peasantry of England_**  
Edited by **Robert Bell**  
Transcribed from the **1857 John W. Parker and Son edition**. citeturn389077view0

The page confirms **“The Plain-Dealing Man”** appears under **Poems**, starting at page 11, and notes that the oldest copy known to the editor was a black-letter print by **T. Vere**, who was living in **1609**. citeturn389077view0

## Best use for your Gilbert project

This source actually strengthens the Gilbert-style direction.

The collection frames these works as **popular poems, ballads, and songs preserved among ordinary people**, including moral poems, comic songs, rural songs, and pieces “from grave to gay, from lively to severe.” citeturn389077view0 That makes **“The Plain-Dealing Man”** suitable not as a solemn literary poem, but as a **public-facing character song**: moral, repetitive, comic, direct, and performable.

## Best genre choice

### **Primary recommendation**
**Gilbertian comic operetta / Victorian music-hall moral patter song**

This is the strongest fit because the poem already has:

| Feature in original | Song value |
|---|---|
| Repeated moral refrain | Easy chorus/hook |
| List of bad social types | Patter-song catalogue material |
| Self-righteous speaker | Comic character voice |
| Plain moral lesson | Gilbert-style satirical lecture |
| Old proverb structure | Good opening setup |

## Best version to adapt

Use a **compressed lyrical adaptation**, not the full poem.

Best structure:

```text
[VERSE 1]
Introduce the proverb: plain dealing is rarer than gold.

[CHORUS]
A polished version of:
’Tis the excellent thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

[VERSE 2]
Attack swaggerers, flatterers, hypocrites.

[VERSE 3]
Attack liars, bribe-takers, cheats, thieves.

[PATTER BRIDGE]
Rapid comic list of every dishonest type.

[FINAL VERSE]
Advice: keep good company, save money, keep conscience clean.

[FINAL CHORUS]
Bigger ensemble finish.
```

## Best working title

**“The Plain-Dealing Man”** is already strong.

Alternative Gilbert-style titles:

- **“The Most Excellent Plain-Dealing Man”**
- **“A Jewel Most Rare”**
- **“Plain Dealing Is Best”**
- **“The Honest Man’s Defence”**

## Suggested musical style

```text
[STYLE]
Victorian comic operetta, Gilbert-and-Sullivan-inspired music-hall patter song, jaunty 6/8 or brisk 2/4, theatrical baritone lead, witty moral satire, ensemble chorus responses, light orchestra with piano, strings, woodwinds, brass stabs, comic rhythmic accents, increasingly fast patter bridge, grand mock-serious finale.
```

## Strongest chorus adaptation

```text
For I’ll make it appear,
As plainly as I can,
There’s nothing half so rare
As a plain-dealing man.

Let silver lose its shine,
Let gold fall from the hand,
The jewel of the world
Is a plain-dealing man.
```

## My judgement

For the **Gilbert project**, this should become a **comic moral catalogue song**.

Not folk.  
Not serious ballad.  
Not modern pop.

The best version is a **theatrical character piece** where the singer proudly presents himself as honest while condemning everyone else in society. That gives it humour, rhythm, and stage function.

Where you had labels like:

```text
baritone operetta vocal / hip-hop spoken mix
```

That can confuse Suno because it may not know which vocal should dominate.

The better rule is:

```text
main vocal first, secondary rhythm second
```

Example:

```text
cheat and thief verse,
baritone operetta vocal as main voice, hip-hop rhythm underneath only
```

Instead of:

```text
baritone operetta vocal / hip-hop spoken mix
```

For the **final verse**, the best fix is:

```text
final verse,
baritone operetta vocal as main voice, hip-hop spoken emphasis on practical advice lines, moral resolution in stronger baritone
```

That gives Suno a clear hierarchy:

1. **Main vocal**
2. **Secondary flavour**
3. **Production support**

parts:
## Best version to make it a song

The **best version is not the full original poem unchanged**. It is too long and too sermon-like for a modern song.

The strongest musical version would be a **compressed adaptation** built around the refrain:

> **’Tis the excellent thing in the world  
> To be a plain-dealing man**

That refrain is the hook. The song should keep the old moral-ballad flavour but reduce the verses into selected “character attacks”:

1. **boasters / swaggerers**
2. **false swearers / liars**
3. **bribe takers**
4. **cheaters / thieves**
5. **final moral advice**

That gives the song shape instead of becoming a long list.

---

## Best genre

### Best fit: **Victorian music-hall / comic moral ballad**

This fits the **Gilbert project** best if you mean a Gilbert & Sullivan / W. S. Gilbert-style piece.

Why it works:

- The poem already has a **comic moral lecturer** voice.
- It attacks social types: hypocrites, gossips, bribe-takers, cheats.
- The repeated refrain can become a **catchy chorus**.
- The speaker sounds self-righteous but slightly ridiculous, which is very Gilbertian.
- It can be staged as a character song: one man presenting himself as “the honest man” while judging everyone else.

### Secondary fit: **patter-song / satirical catalogue song**

This would be more comic and faster.

The repeated “O fie upon…” sections could become a patter catalogue:

> O fie upon the bribe-taker,  
> oath-breaker, coin-shaker,  
> back-door favour-maker,  
> truth-bending man...

This would sync strongly with Gilbert-style social satire.

---

## Suggested song concept for the Gilbert project

### Title

**“The Plain-Dealing Man”**

### Character

A pompous but sincere lower-middle-class moralist.  
He believes he is the last honest man in a corrupt world.

### Tone

Comic, moral, theatrical, slightly self-important.

### Musical style

- **Light operetta / Victorian music hall**
- 6/8 or jaunty 2/4
- March-like chorus
- Increasingly fast verse sections
- Ensemble can echo the refrain mock-seriously

---

## Best structure

```text
[INTRO]
Short spoken or sung setup:
“A crotchet comes into my mind...”

[VERSE 1]
He introduces the proverb:
Plain dealing is rarer than gold.

[CHORUS]
For this I make it clear as I can,
The finest thing in life is a plain-dealing man.

[VERSE 2]
Attack on swaggerers, flatterers, liars.

[CHORUS]

[VERSE 3]
Attack on bribe-takers, cheats, thieves.

[CHORUS]

[BRIDGE / PATTER SECTION]
Fast comic list of every dishonest type.

[FINAL VERSE]
Advice to young men:
avoid bad company, save your money, keep conscience clean.

[FINAL CHORUS]
Bigger, ensemble, comic-moral finish.
```

---

## What I would avoid

Do **not** make it:

- a solemn folk ballad only
- a modern pop song
- a dark dramatic aria
- a fully literal setting of every stanza

The material is moral and repetitive, so if treated too seriously it may become dull. It needs **comic theatrical energy**.

---

## Best adapted chorus

A stronger singable chorus could be:

```text
For I’ll make it appear,
As plainly as I can,
There’s nothing half so rare
As a plain-dealing man.
Let silver go to rust,
Let gold slip through the hand,
The jewel of the world
Is a plain-dealing man.
```

This keeps the old idea but makes it more musical.

---

## My recommendation

For the Gilbert project, make it a **comic operetta character song**:

> **Genre:** Victorian music-hall operetta / Gilbertian patter ballad  
> **Mood:** witty, moral, theatrical, satirical  
> **Voice:** pompous honest man condemning a corrupt society  
> **Best use:** Act I character introduction or comic moral set-piece  

The refrain is strong enough to become one of the project’s recurring comic themes.

My recommendation was always:

When you asked:

I understood **“full lyrics”** as:

I did **not** understand it as:

```text
[TITLE]
THE PLAIN-DEALING MAN

[SOURCE NOTE]
From Ancient Poems, Ballads and Songs of the Peasantry of England,

[ORIGINAL TEXT]

A crotchet comes into my mind
Concerning a proverb of old,
Plain dealing’s a jewel most rare,
And more precious than silver or gold:
And therefore with patience give ear,
And listen to what here is penned,
These verses were written on purpose
The honest man’s cause to defend.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

Yet some are so impudent grown,
They’ll domineer, vapour, and swagger,
And say that the plain-dealing man
Was born to die a beggar:
But men that are honestly given
Do such evil actions detest,
And every one that is well-minded
Will say that plain dealing is best.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

For my part I am a poor man,
And sometimes scarce muster a shilling,
Yet to live upright in the world,
Heaven knows I am wondrous willing.
Although that my clothes be threadbare,
And my calling be simple and poor,
Yet will I endeavour myself
To keep off the wolf from the door.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

And now, to be brief in discourse,
In plain terms I’ll tell you my mind;
My qualities you shall all know,
And to what my humour’s inclined:
I hate all dissembling base knaves
And pickthanks whoever they be,
And for painted-faced drabs, and such like,
They shall never get penny of me.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

Nor can I abide any tongues
That will prattle and prate against reason,
About that which doth not concern them;
Which thing is no better than treason.
Wherefore I’d wish all that do hear me
Not to meddle with matters of state,
Lest they be in question called for it,
And repent them when it is too late.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon spiteful neighbours,
Whose malicious humours are bent,
And do practise and strive every day
To wrong the poor innocent.
By means of such persons as they,
There hath many a good mother’s son
Been utterly brought to decay,
Their wives and their children undone.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon forsworn knaves,
That do no conscience make
To swear and forswear themselves
At every third word they do speak:
So they may get profit and gain,
They care not what lies they do tell;
Such cursed dissemblers as they
Are worse than the devils of hell.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon greedy bribe takers,
’Tis pity they ever drew breath,
For they, like to base caterpillars,
Devour up the fruits of the earth.
They’re apt to take money with both hands,
On one side and also the other,
And care not what men they undo,
Though it be their own father or brother.

Therefore I will make it appear,
And show very good reasons I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

O fie upon cheaters and thieves,
That liveth by fraud and deceit;
The gallows do for such blades groan,
And the hangmen do for their clothes wait.
Though poverty be a disgrace,
And want is a pitiful grief,
’Tis better to go like a beggar
Than to ride in a cart like a thief.

For this I will make it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

And now let all honest men judge,
If such men as I have here named
For their wicked and impudent dealings,
Deserveth not much to be blamed.
And now here, before I conclude,
One item to the world I will give,
Which may direct some the right way,
And teach them the better to live.

For now I have made it appear,
And many men witness it can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

1. I’ th’ first place I’d wish you beware
What company you come in,
For those that are wicked themselves
May quickly tempt others to sin.

2. If youths be inducèd with wealth,
And have plenty of silver and gold,
I’d wish them keep something in store,
To comfort them when they are old.

3. I have known many young prodigals,
Which have wasted their money so fast,
That they have been driven in want,
And were forcèd to beg at the last.

4. I’d wish all men bear a good conscience,
And in all their actions be just;
For he’s a false varlet indeed
That will not be true to his trust.

And now to conclude my new song,
And draw to a perfect conclusion,
I have told you what is in my mind,
And what is my firm resolution.

For this I have made it appear,
And prove by experience I can,
’Tis the excellen’st thing in the world
To be a plain-dealing man.

Yes, that is a good idea. It can reduce characters **without creating confusion**, as long as the structure order is clear.

Best approach:

1. **Put one global style block**
2. **List the vocal/production modes once**
3. **Give the section order separately**
4. **Use short labels in the lyrics**, such as `intro, baritone`, `verse 2, patter rap`, `chorus, ensemble`

That is usually clearer for Suno than repeating long production notes in every heading.

## My recommendation

Use this **vocal map + structure order** format for the **style/structure prompt**, then keep the lyrics themselves with only short section labels.

It should be less confusing than long repeated headings, because Suno sees the rules once and then follows the section order.
